clue.text: Carriage that carried away Rachael Wardle

definitions.meaning: a light two-wheeled covered car once used in Ireland and Australia
in Dickens's Pickwick Papers the adventurer Alfred of that name elopes with the spinster Rachael Wardle

explanation.surface: A question about which vehicle bore off a Dickens heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is the eloping rogue from The Pickwick Papers, read as the thing that carried her away.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a small horse-drawn vehicle, and the surname of the Pickwick rogue who runs off with Miss Wardle.

clue.text: His wife had no problem with left-overs !

definitions.text: His wife had no problem with left-overs !

parts.words: His wife had no problem with left-overs
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme he could eat no fat and his wife no lean, so between them the plate was licked clean

explanation.surface: A remark about a wife who happily eats up what is left.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme husband ate no fat, his wife no lean, so nothing was left on the platter.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme man who would eat no fat, whose wife ate the fat he left.

clue.text: Figures that leave one cold?

definitions.meaning: things that make one numb, as cold does

explanation.surface: Statistics that fail to excite.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as 'more numb' or 'things that numb', from numb.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: digits, and things that make one go numb with cold.

clue.text: Observer gets warning !

definitions.meaning: a sentry or watchman posted to keep watch
a shout telling a fellow to beware, two words and 'man'

explanation.surface: A watcher receives an alert.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a sentry keeping watch, and a cry telling a fellow to take care.

clue.text: Test implement of a renowned curate ?

definitions.text: Test implement of a renowned curate ?

parts.words: Test implement of a renowned curate
parts.note: the Punch cartoon curate, served a bad boiled breakfast, said it was good in parts; the tool he tested it with is meant

explanation.surface: A query about the tool a famous clergyman used for his trial.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'renowned curate' is the one in the 1895 Punch cartoon whose breakfast was 'good in parts'; the small utensil for eating it is what tested it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small utensil for eating from a boiled shell is what the cartoon clergyman would have used on his breakfast.

clue.text: Where Norval's father fed his flocks

definitions.text: Where Norval's father fed his flocks

parts.words: Where Norval's father fed his flocks
parts.note: in John Home's play Douglas the hero says 'My name is Norval; on the ___ hills my father feeds his flocks'

explanation.surface: A question of geography from an old Scottish tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: A famous recitation piece from John Home's 1756 tragedy Douglas names the Scottish mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish mountain range named in the hero's speech in Home's tragedy Douglas.

clue.text: One can say nothing of this protein source

indicators.note: to can is to process and repack, so the letters of say and nothing are worked into a new order

parts.note: zero, the round letter O

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that nothing can be said about a bean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' signals that SAY and O (nothing) are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: The bean of an Asian legume is a rich vegetable source of protein.

clue.text: The sting's in the tail in the matter of expulsion

definitions.text: The sting's in the tail in the matter of expulsion

parts.words: The sting's in the tail in the matter of expulsion
parts.note: the word for an expulsion ends in the letters s-t-i-n-g, so its sting is literally at its tail

explanation.surface: A proverb about nasty surprises applied to throwing someone out.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the sting is in the tail' is literally true of the word meaning expulsion, whose last five letters spell sting.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of driving someone out of a position is an expulsion.

clue.text: Milton urged her to haste

parts.note: Milton's L'Allegro calls 'Haste thee, ___, and bring with thee Jest and youthful Jollity'

explanation.surface: A literary note about whom Milton hurried along.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in L'Allegro addresses a mythological maiden spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden spirit of nature is the figure Milton's poem summons to hurry.

clue.text: " Farewell ! thou art too for my possessing " (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: " Farewell ! thou art too for my possessing " (Shakespeare)

parts.words: Farewell ! thou art too for my possessing
parts.note: Shakespeare's Sonnet 87 opens with this line, the gap being an adjective meaning costly or beloved

explanation.surface: A gapped quotation: Shakespeare's farewell to a loved one.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 87 opens on a pun: the beloved is too costly and too beloved to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: The word meaning both beloved and expensive completes the sonnet's opening line.

clue.text: Settle down to make music

explanation.surface: An instruction to calm down so that one can write music.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: to calm oneself, and to create a musical work.

clue.text: Cure for madness found in asylums

indicators.note: to found is to cast metal afresh, so the letters of the next word are recast into a new shape

explanation.surface: A remedy for insanity discovered in mental hospitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' looks like 'located inside', but the plant's letters are a rearrangement of ASYLUMS, not a run within it.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant madwort was once thought to calm rage; its Greek name means 'without frenzy'.

clue.text: Swift writing ?

parts.note: reads as a work by Jonathan Swift, but means rapid shorthand script

explanation.surface: A remark about the works of Jonathan Swift.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S on 'Swift' suggests the satirist; the clue means quick writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorthand is written at speed, and this word names a shorthand record.

clue.text: with the spoils of time (Gray)

parts.note: fill the gap in Gray's Elegy line '... with the spoils of time did ne'er unroll'

explanation.surface: A gapped quotation from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word opens the line about Knowledge's ample page, 'Rich with the spoils of time', in Gray's Elegy.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning abundantly supplied or wealthy completes the poet's phrase.

clue.text: Skye ?

parts.note: the Hebridean island is also a breed of terrier

explanation.surface: A single query about the Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Skye is an island and a terrier breed, so one Skye fits both halves of the London district's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is both an island and a breed of terrier; the London district name combines island and hounds.

clue.text: A girl of stone ?

parts.note: a female first name that is also the name of the inscribed Egyptian slab in the British Museum

explanation.surface: A question about a girl made of stone, like a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: The decoding slab found in Egypt in 1799 bears a name that is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name shared with the famous trilingual inscribed stone that unlocked hieroglyphs.

clue.text: Classically, the height of the legal profession

definitions.text: Classically, the height of the legal profession

parts.words: Classically, the height of the legal profession
parts.note: in ancient Athens the supreme court sat on a hill named after Ares

explanation.surface: A remark about the summit of a career in law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'height' is literal: the Athenian council and court met on Ares' hill.
explanation.definitionFit: The hill of Ares in Athens, seat of the city's highest court in ancient times.

clue.text: They get their rights in the guise of portents

parts.note: in the role or character of, which is 'as'
omens are signs

explanation.surface: People granted rights while appearing as omens.
explanation.walkthrough: In law the persons to whom rights are transferred are called by this plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, assignees are the people to whom property or rights are transferred.

clue.text: Describes the Dance of the Daffodils

definitions.text: Describes the Dance of the Daffodils

parts.words: Describes the Dance of the Daffodils
parts.note: Wordsworth's daffodils were seen 'tossing their heads in ___ dance'

explanation.surface: A question about the poet's word for the flowers' movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' has the flowers 'tossing their heads in ___ dance'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means lively and brisk, the word Wordsworth applies to his flowers' dance.

clue.text: A dainty dish for Labour returning in time!

indicators.note: one piece is set inside the word for time

parts.note: the word taken as written

indicators.note: coming back, so the abbreviation for Labour is read backwards

parts.note: LAB is the short form for Britain's Labour Party

explanation.surface: A political joke about Labour coming back into power just in time for a feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns LAB into BAL, which goes 'in' TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum-shaped mould of savoury mixture, a refined dish served as an entree.

clue.text: He's out of this world

parts.note: literally from another planet, rather than marvellous

explanation.surface: Praise for someone wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of this world' usually means superb; read literally, it is a visitor from the red planet.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhabitant of the fourth planet is literally not of the Earth.

clue.text: Lodging for the lieutenant in thinnest silk

indicators.note: the officer's abbreviation sits within the word for the fabric

parts.note: a very fine, transparent fabric is called sheer
Lt is the standard abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: An officer's billet made of the flimsiest silk.
explanation.definitionFit: A place to stay, cover from the weather, is a refuge or accommodation.

clue.text: Where do we go from here?

definitions.text: Where do we go from here?

parts.words: Where do we go from here
parts.note: a question of what to do next, read as asking for a direction away from this place

explanation.surface: A rueful question about the next step.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom asks what next; literally, going from here is going to that place.
explanation.definitionFit: An old adverb meaning to that place, the opposite of hither.

clue.text: Indicating the needful

parts.note: naming exactly what is required, as in a builder's list of requirements

explanation.surface: Showing what is necessary.
explanation.definitionFit: To state precisely what is required is to set down the requirements in detail.

clue.text: Get wind of the doctor ?

parts.note: the strong south-easterly at the tip of Africa is nicknamed the doctor, for clearing the air

explanation.surface: A hint about learning of a physician's whereabouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get wind of' means hear about, but here the Doctor is a wind: the bracing summer south-easter at Cape Town.
explanation.definitionFit: The south-easterly wind at Cape Town is called the Cape Doctor; the headland gives its name.

clue.text: About a wing in the salaried staff

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: Office staff about to join a wing of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to a wing, from Latin ala.

clue.text: Gimbling time for toves

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky opens with the slithy toves who did gyre and gimble at a certain hour

explanation.surface: Nonsense about when Carroll's creatures do their thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Humpty Dumpty explains the nonsense word as four o'clock in the afternoon, the time for broiling dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's opening nonsense word for the hour when the toves gyre and gimble in the wabe.

clue.text: One was an early submarine traveller

definitions.text: One was an early submarine traveller

parts.words: One was an early submarine traveller
parts.note: Jonah, swallowed by the great fish, travelled beneath the sea

explanation.surface: A remark about a pioneer of underwater travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'submarine' means simply 'under the sea': Jonah, an Old Testament seer, journeyed inside the whale.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonah was a biblical seer who spent three days inside a great fish under the sea.

clue.text: Tart for statesmen in conclave

definitions.meaning: a pastry tart with almond filling bears this name
a formal assembly of delegates or legislators

explanation.surface: A pastry served to politicians meeting in private.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: an almond-filled pastry, and a formal assembly of national representatives.

clue.text: But at home in Battersea?

parts.note: Battersea Dogs Home in London takes in lost animals, so being lost would there count as being home

explanation.surface: A paradox about being at home in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Battersea Dogs Home, in south London, shelters lost dogs; something wandering is not at home, 'but' it would be at home there.
explanation.definitionFit: Lost or off course; a stray dog is one that has wandered, and Battersea is where it ends up.
